sentences.text: There's a reason this young painter dared to look like Christ.
This is the Self-Portrait at Twenty-Eight, painted by Albrecht Dürer in 1500.
Most people see it as stunning arrogance, or even blasphemy.
His frontal pose, his gaze and his blessing hand all copy pictures of Christ.
And the picture seems to agree.
His long hair and his calm eyes look straight out at you.
He painted it brown, not his real reddish blond.
According to a later woodcut by Sebald Beham, this exact face became the face of Christ.
In the next century, Johann Georg Vischer used it for Christ again.
It isn't Dürer pretending to be Christ.
It's Christ who ended up wearing Dürer's face.
So did he copy Christ, or did Christ end up copying him?

meta.title: He Painted Himself Like Christ... Then Christ Got HIS Face #history #art

sources.claim: Self-Portrait (or Self-Portrait at Twenty-Eight) is a panel painting by the German Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer.
The self-portrait is considered remarkable because of its resemblance to contemporary representations of Christ, which could be interpreted as a feat of either stunning arrogance or blasphemy.

The similarities with the conventions of religious painting include the positioning of his hands which seem to be in the act of blessing, the manner of his direct gaze, and the sober and earthy tones.
Dürer has rendered himself in this manner, and gives himself brown hair, despite his other self-portraits showing his hair as reddish-blond.
The painting so closely follows the conventions of late medieval religious art that it was used as the basis for depictions of Christ in a woodcut by Sebald Beham of c. 1520.
In the next century, the face was used for Christ again, in a Christ and the Woman Taken in Adultery of 1637 by Johann Georg Vischer.
